# The real cost is more than the purchase price

Build a realistic budget for accommodation, everyday care and the unexpected.

## Separate purchase price from lifetime care

The initial price of a parrot is only one part of ownership. Start by identifying the exact species and suitable equipment rather than comparing birds on price alone. A smaller bird still needs an appropriate environment and veterinary care.

Request a clear price for the specific individual and an explanation of what is included. Our UK buying enquiry hub explains the information to confirm before proceeding.

## Plan the setup budget

Allow for accommodation, appropriate perches, feeding equipment, transport and safe enrichment. Large parrots may require robust equipment and more usable space. Assess the actual products and arrangements needed for your chosen species.

Do not buy an enclosure solely because it is advertised for parrots. Check size, usable layout, bar spacing and suitability with an informed source. See the housing guide before finalising the setup.

## Account for recurring expenses

Budget for food, cleaning supplies, replacement toys and worn equipment. Plan for routine veterinary care and ask local avian practices about their services and costs. Prices vary by location, provider and the bird’s needs, so obtain relevant quotations.

Also consider care when you travel or cannot follow the usual routine. Identify suitable help and establish its availability rather than treating it as an afterthought.

## Leave room for uncertainty

Unexpected health concerns and changes in household circumstances can affect costs. Keep a practical reserve and think about long-term arrangements, particularly for birds that may be companions for decades.

Money is only part of the commitment. Daily time and consistency matter too. Use the species selection guide to check whether the financial and practical requirements fit your home.

## Turn the care plan into a realistic budget

Before committing, make two separate budget views: expected ownership expenses and an emergency reserve. The first is money you plan to spend as part of ordinary care; the second is savings deliberately kept available for a sudden veterinary need or another urgent disruption. Do not quietly count the reserve as though it were a predictable monthly bill, and do not assume insurance, if chosen, removes the need for accessible funds. Compare the policy exclusions, excesses and limits directly with the insurer.

For expected expenses, list the actual setup needed for your selected species: appropriately sized accommodation, secure fittings, perches, feeding equipment and safe enrichment. Price suitable products rather than using a generic “parrot cage” figure. Add recurring food and cleaning supplies, replacement toys or chew materials, routine veterinary appointments, and travel or care arrangements when you are away. Ask local veterinary practices and providers for current quotations; charges vary by location, service and the individual bird. Large equipment may also need periodic repair or replacement, so allow for wear instead of treating the initial setup as permanent.

Keep a separate line for the bird’s purchase quote. Request current availability and pricing for the specific individual and confirm what, if anything, is included. Contact Crownwing Parrots for current availability and pricing. A purchase quote is not a lifetime-cost estimate: the commercial purchase information belongs on parrot prices in the UK, while this guide concerns ongoing ownership. Revisit your budget after confirming the exact species, accommodation, diet and veterinary plan, before paying or arranging transport.

## Budget for continuity of care

Consider a week when you are away, unwell or unable to provide the ordinary routine. Identify a capable backup keeper, ask what care they can actually provide, and obtain any relevant provider quotation. Add planned paid care to your researched ownership estimates rather than assuming family help will always be available.

Keep clear instructions about familiar foods, secure accommodation, supervision and how to contact the veterinary practice. Confirm arrangements with the person concerned and revisit them when your circumstances change. Consider a future move, changed work pattern or loss of a regular carer, not only a short holiday. A continuity plan is a practical responsibility, not an advertised Crownwing boarding or transport service.
